title: The Business Case for PBAC
subtitle: Risk, cost, compliance — and when not to adopt
content:
💰 The Cost of Scattered AuthZ

  • Breach cost: BOLA and tenant leakage are data-breach categories with notification, churn, and regulatory exposure.
  • Audit cost: answering who can access what? across N services with inline checks is a quarter-long project. With centralized policy it is a query.
  • Velocity cost: every new endpoint re-implements checks; every incident fix must be ported N times.
  • People cost: only the original author understands service #7's checks. Policy-as-code is readable by the next team.

🏛️ Compliance Maps to Policy Artifacts (Partially)

SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, GDPR, and the EU AI Act all ask variants of: define access rules, enforce least privilege, review them, log decisions. Versioned policy + decision logs + periodic access reviews support controls like SOC 2 CC6/CC7, ISO A.5/A.8, HIPAA §164.308/312, GDPR Art. 5/25/32, and AI Act logging/human-oversight — but do not alone satisfy them. HIPAA still needs administrative/physical safeguards + risk analysis; GDPR still needs DPIAs, subject rights, breach notification, minimization; the AI Act still needs risk management, data governance, and robustness. Map control-by-control; residual work (reviews, DPIAs, incident process, tagging stewardship) is real labor, not "almost free".

🗺️ The Platform Landscape (Vendor-Neutral)

  • OPA: general-purpose engine; APIs, K8s (Gatekeeper), CI (Conftest), data filtering. You host it.
  • Cedar / Amazon Verified Permissions: app-focused language + managed PDP; schema-first with formal verification tooling.
  • OpenFGA: Zanzibar-style relationship engine for sharing graphs. You host it.
  • Immuta: data-plane governance: subscription + masking/row policies on Snowflake/Databricks/etc.
  • PlainID: enterprise authorization plane: visual policy, PDP APIs, SaaS connectors, AI-agent guardrails.

Also in the market (not full lessons — honest placement):

  • Styra DAS: managed OPA control plane (bundles, decisions, audit) — choose over self-hosted OPA when you want OPA semantics without running the fleet. Bill: managed platform (confirm current pricing). Exit: your Rego ports, but re-point sidecars/bundles, replay decision-audit, and rebuild DAS-specific distribution config.
  • Aserto: managed PDP + directory with framework authorizers — choose for drop-in app integration speed. Bill: managed per-decision/seat (confirm current pricing). Exit: OPA-compatible policies port, but directory data and Edge authorizer bindings need remapping.
  • Warrant: Zanzibar-style managed API (objects, relations, warrants) — choose over OpenFGA when you want the relationship model without operating it; exit means re-homing tuples + model, so keep an export routine from day one.
  • Ory Keto: self-hosted Zanzibar-style engine in the Ory ecosystem — choose when you already run Ory (Kratos/Hydra) and want one identity+authZ vendor. Bill: your ops instead of a vendor invoice; same tuple-portability caveat as Warrant.

Rule of thumb: managed buys speed, self-hosted buys control, open languages buy exits. Every managed pick above rents its decision path — price the exit (export routines, portable policies) before you need it.

This course is not a vendor pitch: every platform lesson names the lock-in, the bill, and the exit path.

🚫 When NOT to Adopt (Honesty Section)

  • Three roles, one app, no auditors → policy file + tests, no platform.
  • No owner for policy content → a PDP without maintained policy is shelfware with latency.
  • Latency budget under ~5ms p99 with no cache tolerance → decide locally or cache decisions; measure first.

questions.question: What is the most expensive property of scattered if-statement authorization?

options.text: No single auditable answer to 'who can access what' — every review is N-service archaeology
If-statements use too much CPU
If-statements cannot check roles
Junior developers cannot read if-statements

questions.explanation: The cost is systemic: unauditable, untestable-as-a-whole, and N-times porting of every fix. CPU is irrelevant; comprehension at estate scale is the bill.

questions.question: An auditor asks for evidence of least-privilege enforcement. What do you show in a PBAC estate?

options.text: Versioned policy + decision logs + periodic access reviews
The OIDC configuration showing MFA is enabled
The password complexity setting
A verbal assurance from engineering

questions.explanation: Policy history shows what the rules were; decision logs show what was enforced; reviews show humans still check. That triple is the compliance artifact.

questions.question: Which platform fits warehouse column-masking and row filters on Snowflake/Databricks?

options.text: Immuta-style data policies (subscription + masking/row rules by tag)
OpenFGA relationship tuples
Kubernetes admission control
JWT signature verification

questions.explanation: Data-plane governance (mask/tag/row-filter at query time) is Immuta's lane. OpenFGA answers object-sharing questions; K8s admission answers deploy-time questions.

questions.question: Your estate shows versioned policy, decision logs, and quarterly access reviews. The GDPR auditor now asks about deletion handling and DPIAs. Best response?

options.text: Produce the DPIA register and deletion runbooks — policy artifacts never covered those; map control-by-control
Claim the PDP logs alone satisfy GDPR
Delete the decision logs to minimize stored data
Show the login page again, more slowly

questions.explanation: Residual work is real: DPIAs, subject rights, breach notification, and minimization sit outside authorization. Evidence supports a control; it is not the control.

questions.question: What does least privilege require of a policy set over time?

options.text: Regular reviews that shrink grants to what is actually used
Granting admin to everyone for simplicity
Never changing policies after launch
Deleting all logs to save storage

questions.explanation: Least privilege is a process, not a launch state: grants decay toward usage, exceptions expire, and reviews remove what drifted.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly matched to its sweet spot?

options.text: OpenFGA → per-object sharing graphs; Immuta-style → warehouse masking
JWTs → warehouse masking; OpenFGA → column masking
Gatekeeper → SaaS user provisioning
PlainID → container image scanning

questions.explanation: Relationship engines answer sharing questions; data-plane governance answers masking questions. Mismatching them is the classic platform misbuy.

questions.question: Quarterly review finds 40% of grants unused. Correct response?

options.text: Expire or remove them; require re-justification for exceptions
Keep them — removal feels risky
Convert everything to admin for simplicity
Review less often to save time

questions.explanation: Least privilege decays without pruning. Unused grants are breach surface with zero business value.

questions.question: The cheapest authorization to operate across 50 services is…

options.text: One policy plane with per-service enforcement, tested once
Fifty hand-rolled check sets
No authorization at all
One shared admin password

questions.explanation: Centralize the decision, distribute enforcement. N implementations means N audits, N ports of every fix.
